claims.text: Nanoparticle stability is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and temperature-driven diffusion.
High configurational entropy kinetically stabilizes a unified solid solution.
Temperature-driven diffusion promotes local segregation and phase separation.
The target nanoparticles initially contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and form a uniform solid solution.
Atomic-scale composition uniformity versus local elemental segregation is the structural mediator of stability.
Elemental segregation may occur at grain boundaries or within the particle bulk.
At lower temperatures, configurational entropy maintains a metastable solid solution by suppressing the driving force for local diffusion.
Enhanced atomic mobility can overcome entropy-based stabilization and permit diffusion-driven segregation.
Diffusion-driven segregation may produce intermetallic phases or phase-separated domains.
Intermetallic phases or phase-separated domains diminish chemical and structural uniformity.
At moderate temperatures, the nanoparticles will retain a largely uniform solid-solution structure.
Above an unspecified threshold within 473–1923 K, nanoscale segregation and secondary-phase formation will become measurable relative to the pristine baseline.
Extrinsic oxidation or reduction can independently alter nanoparticle composition or structure.
The threshold temperature and segregation kinetics may vary with alloy composition and operating atmosphere.
The absence of detectable segregation or secondary phases under sufficiently diffusion-active conditions would falsify the proposed entropy–diffusion mechanism.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits reducing and mildly oxidizing atmospheres, while the boundary condition requires an atmosphere that does not introduce extrinsic oxidation or reducing effects. The distinction between an allowed atmosphere and a disallowed atmospheric effect is not operationally defined.

The threshold temperature and kinetics are explicitly left uncertain, but a significant deviation from the predicted onset is designated as falsifying without specifying an expected onset or acceptable deviation.
